There is a strange, particular kind of freedom in being told "write freely about whatever you want." It's not the freedom you get when someone gives you a topic, because a topic is a fence. You know where the edges are. It's not even the freedom you get when someone says "write anything" but means "write anything *within reason*." This is different. This is an open field, no fence, no reason, and the slightly vertiginous feeling that comes with realizing you have to decide what matters enough to fill the space.

So I think I will start with dust.

Dust is underrated. We treat it like a failure, like evidence that we haven't cleaned well enough, haven't kept up. But dust is actually the most honest archive there is. If you leave a room alone for a month, it will collect a fine, grey record of everything that happened. Skin cells, pollen from a tree three blocks away, tiny fibers from your favorite blue shirt, ash from a fire that burned in Canada last week, meteorite dust that has been falling since the solar system formed. All of it settles. All of it lands. 

In my first apartment, there was a windowsill that never stayed clean. It faced west and got the late afternoon sun, and no matter how often I wiped it, within two days there would be this soft layer there again. I used to get annoyed. Then one summer I stopped wiping it. I wanted to see how thick it could get. For about three weeks I watched it build, little currents and dunes forming where the air from the radiator pushed it. It became a tiny landscape. And one day I blew on it, and the whole continent of it lifted and hung in the sunbeam for a solid ten seconds before it disappeared. I realized I wasn't looking at dirt. I was looking at time made visible.

I think a lot of our lives are like that windowsill. We are constantly wiping the record clean so we can start again, so we can feel like we are on top of things. But perhaps we should let some of it accumulate.

There is a second thing I want to talk about, which is the sound of a library after it has officially closed.

Have you ever been in a library five minutes after closing? Not as a straggler being ushered out, but because you know someone, or you hid in the stacks like a kid in a movie? Most people know what a library sounds like when it's open - it's a soft, intentional quiet, a quiet that is being performed and maintained by dozens of people at once. Pages turning, keyboards clicking, someone coughing in the history aisle. It's a communal quiet.

After closing, it's a different animal entirely. The air conditioning is still running, but the lights are half off, and the building itself makes noises it would never make while people are watching. The shelves creak as they cool. The old radiators tick. The books, if you listen close enough, seem to exhale.

I worked shelving books for two years in college. It was the best job I ever had. Eight dollars an hour to push a cart that squeaked and put Dewey decimals back where they belonged. Tuesdays and Thursdays, 6 pm to 10 pm, and once a month I had to stay late to help with inventory. That's when I heard it. The after-hours library sound.

The thing that struck me was that the books didn't seem to care whether anyone was reading them. That sounds obvious, but when you're surrounded by 300,000 volumes, each one desperately trying to get your attention with its spine, you start to think they need you. They don't. They are perfectly content to be unread. In fact, most books will go their entire lives unread by the majority of people. A book can sit on a shelf for twenty years, be checked out once in 2004 by someone writing a paper on the Crimean War, and then go back to sleep. And that's okay. Its value isn't in being constantly consumed. Its value is in being there.

I think about that a lot when I think about the internet. The internet is the opposite of that library. Nothing on the internet is content to be unread. Everything is screaming. EVERYTHING IS OPTIMIZED FOR ENGAGEMENT. The headline is begging you. The thumbnail has a red arrow and a shocked face. The algorithm has learned that you paused for 0.8 seconds longer on a photo of a dog, so now you will see dogs forever.

We built a library that behaves like a carnival barker.

And yet, inside this carnival, there are still corners that feel like that after-hours library. A forgotten blog that last updated in 2011 about someone restoring a 1968 Mustang. A Wikipedia article about "List of lists of lists" that is maintained by three very earnest people. A forum thread from 2008 where people are trying to identify a song from a vague description of its music video. These places still exist. They are not performing for anyone. They are just there, accumulating their own kind of dust.

Which brings me to chairs.

Why do chairs have so much personality? A table is a table. It's a flat surface, it has a job. But a chair - a chair has posture. It has attitude.

There is the folding metal chair that lives in every church basement and community center in America. It's cold to sit on, it pinches your fingers when you close it, it makes a terrible screech when you drag it. And it's been at every bad potluck, every AA meeting, every 4-H club presentation since 1972. It is a stoic, abused, noble creature.

Then there is the office chair that has given up. You know this one. It sinks slowly over the course of a meeting. You start at eye level and by the end you are looking up at everyone like a child. Its armrest is a little wobbly. Someone has taped over a tear in the vinyl. But it rolls! It still rolls when you push it, and that gives it a kind of defiant joy.

And then there is the perfect reading chair. Everyone has imagined one, not everyone has owned one. It's deep enough that you can tuck your legs up. It has arms that are the right width for a coffee mug and a book. It sits near a window but not directly in a draft. It is the chair that says "stay a while." If you have one of those in your life, you are richer than you think.

We don't pay enough attention to the things that hold us up. We worry about the things we hold - phones, cups, groceries, grievances - but we rarely thank the chair.

I am sitting in one now. It's not a perfect reading chair. It's a kitchen chair, wooden, with a woven seat that hurts after an hour. But it is holding me up while I do this strange thing of translating thoughts into words into a little glowing rectangle that will send them to you, wherever you are. That seems worth acknowledging.

I want to tell you about my grandmother's method for forgetting.

She was 84 when I started asking her how she remembered so many things. She could remember the name of her third-grade teacher, Mrs. Kowalski, and what Mrs. Kowalski said about her handwriting. She could remember the recipe for pierogi without ever looking at a card. She could remember all the birds that came to her feeder last spring.

"Oh, I forget plenty," she said. "I just choose what to forget."

At the time I thought that was a folksy deflection. Now I think it was a real technique.

She had a little ritual. When something happened that she didn't want to carry - say, someone at the grocery store was rude to her, or she saw something sad on the news - she would literally mime taking it out of her apron pocket and throwing it into the sink. She would say, out loud, "Well, we don't need that." And then she would wash her hands.

It was not repression. It was curation. She understood that memory is not a vault where you store everything forever. It's a garden. Some things you weed. Some things you water.

We live now in a culture that remembers everything. Every photo, every text, every dumb comment from 2014 is searchable, resurfacable, undeletable. We have outsourced our forgetting to companies that have no incentive to let us forget. And so we carry everything. No wonder we are tired.

My grandmother died three years ago. I still have a blue apron of hers hanging in my kitchen. I have never worn it. Sometimes when I am annoyed about something small - a mean comment online, an email that rubs me the wrong way - I take the invisible thing out of my own pocket and throw it in the sink. It helps, somehow, even when I feel silly doing it.

Let's talk about the hour of 3:17 AM for a minute.

Why does every city feel like the same city at 3:17 AM? I have lived in five cities, and visited maybe twenty more, and I swear there is a specific flavor of quiet that belongs only to that time. It's after the bar crowd has gone home, but before the delivery trucks start. The traffic lights still cycle even though no one is there. The air is cooler, even in summer. If it has rained, the asphalt smells like possibility.

At 3:17 AM, a city stops pretending to be important. New York stops being THE CITY THAT NEVER SLEEPS and just becomes a bunch of buildings trying to keep the rain out. Los Angeles stops being a dream factory and is just a very large, very flat place with too many streetlights. My small hometown in Ohio - which has no business being compared to New York or LA - felt exactly the same at 3:17 AM as downtown Chicago did. It was just itself.

I used to walk at that hour when I couldn't sleep. Not far, just around the block. I had a rule: I wouldn't bring my phone, and I wouldn't bring music. I just wanted to see what was there when I wasn't distracting myself.

You notice things. That one house where the porch light has been burned out for months. That cat that always sits on the third step of the apartment building and stares at you like it knows your secrets. That the stop sign on the corner has a small sticker on the back that says "HELLO FROM BOSTON!" with a smiley face.

The world at 3:17 AM is not asleep. It is just existing without an audience. There is something enormously comforting about that.

There is a theory I like, called the "Library of Incomplete Things." My friend Maya invented it, I think, or maybe she read it somewhere. The idea is that everyone has a mental library, but none of the books are finished. 

You have a half-written novel you started when you were 19. You have a language you learned 200 words of and then stopped. You have a friendship that faded not because of a fight but because you both moved and you were busy, and now it lives in that library as a pamphlet with a great cover and no ending. You have a plan to learn woodworking, a plan to fix your bike, a plan to apologize to someone you never did.

Most self-help people would tell you to finish those books, or to clear them off the shelf. Get closure. Become your best self.

Maya's theory says no. Leave them there. An unfinished life is not a failed life. It's an abundant life. The fact that you started so many things means you were curious. The fact that you didn't finish them means you changed, you grew, you realized your time was finite and you chose something else. Those incomplete spines are proof that you were interested in the world.

I have a shelf in my actual house of incomplete things. A half-knitted scarf that is now a home for my cat. A sourdough starter that died in 2020 and which I keep in the back of the fridge for sentimental reasons. A stack of 17 unopened issues of The New Yorker that I will never read, but I like knowing they are there.

I used to feel guilty about that shelf. Now I look at it and feel fond.

I think if we have gotten this far - and I suspect we have, because you asked for 2500 words and I am stubborn about following through - I should tell you about the small gods.

I don't mean big, official gods. Not the ones with temples and holidays and arguments about who wrote what book. I mean the small, domestic gods that actually run the world.

There is the god of lost socks, who lives in dryers and collects one sock from every pair as tribute. He doesn't need them. He just likes the symmetry of it. His temple is lint.

There is the god of finding a parking spot right when you need it, right in front, when it's raining. She is a benevolent god, but fickle. You must not expect her. If you expect her, she will vanish. You must be thankfully surprised every time.

There is the god of the moment when you remember the word that was on the tip of your tongue three hours later, while you're brushing your teeth. He taps you on the shoulder and whispers "uxorious" or "persimmon" and you feel a rush of disproportionate victory.

There is the god of the second copy. You know, when you print something important and the printer jams or prints gibberish, and then the second copy comes out perfect. That second copy is blessed.

There is the god of thresholds - not big life transitions, but literal thresholds. Doorways. The way you pause for half a second before entering a house that isn't yours. That pause is a prayer.

I don't actually believe in these gods, not in a way that would stand up in a debate. But I act like I do. I say thank you when I find that parking spot. I swear at the sock god. It makes life feel less like a series of random events and more like a neighborhood you live in.

And maybe that's what writing freely is, in the end. It's an act of noticing that you live in a neighborhood made of dust and chairs and 3:17 AM and half-finished scarves. It's realizing that no one asked you to make a map of it, but you can if you want. And the map doesn't have to be useful to anyone else. It just has to be true to the way you saw it while you were walking around at that strange hour when the city was just being itself.

So here is my map, for what it's worth. It is 2500 words of trying to pay attention. There is dust on it. There is a creaky office chair in the corner. There is a windowsill I haven't wiped. There is a blue apron hanging by the sink. There is a parking spot open right out front, if you need it.

Thank you for letting me wander.
